headline: Social Security rises 3.6%. Four in five say it's short.
summary: Social Security checks rise 3.6% in January, the biggest raise since 2023. For the average retired worker that is about $76 a month, just over $900 a year. It reaches 76 million people. The number is a formula: July-to-September prices against last year's. AARP polled 1,000 adults over 50, and 80% of recipients said that won't keep up.

cover_question.q: Is a 3.6% raise actually a raise?

cover_answer: No. It catches up on prices, and health care runs ahead.
table_question: Should a raise track prices, or what you actually spend?

5-7.script: Every month the government sends money to people who have retired, like a lot of grandparents. In January those checks get bigger, about $76 more, because food and gas cost more than they did last year. It's like a step stool that grows when the shelf gets higher. Nothing changes for you.
5-7.why: One number, one reason, and a step stool. The formula waits.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script gives one number and one reason: the checks grow because the shop prices grew. The step stool is the anchor, a thing that rises because the shelf did. Expect "does Grandma get more?" If she is retired, yes, in January.

8-12.script: Social Security pays 76 million retired and disabled people every month. Each fall the government compares July-to-September prices with last year's. Prices rose 3.6%, so every check rises 3.6% in January, about $76 for the average retiree. A scoreboard: prices move, checks move the same.
8-12.why: Prices up 3.6%, checks up 3.6%. A rule nobody's hand is on.
8-12.why_long: This age is testing whether adults apply rules the same way every time, so the script hands over a rule with no one's thumb on it: a price count sets the number each fall, by law, and the check follows it. The scoreboard is the mechanism: a change on one side shows up on the other. Expect "who decides?" Nobody. The count does.

13-17.script: Is a 3.6% raise a raise? Checks rise 3.6% in January, matching prices. But people over 65 spend 2.5 times what workers do on health care, and the count follows workers. Four in five recipients told AARP it won't cover it. Second: the fund runs short in six years. Who covers the gap?
13-17.why: Even on paper, short in life. Then who pays in six years.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the raise matches prices, and most of the people getting it say it falls short, because the index counts a worker's shopping and retirees buy more health care. The script asks for both, then who pays when the fund runs short. Expect "will it be there for me?" The articles don't say. Say so.

5-7.q: Why do grandparents get more money?
5-7.a: Things in the shops cost more than last year, so their checks grow a bit to keep up. About $76 a month.

8-12.a: Nobody. A price count, July to September against last year, sets it. By law.
Just over $900 a year. Most people over 50 told AARP it won't keep up with prices.

13-17.q: Is a 3.6% raise actually a raise?
13-17.a: On paper it matches prices. Retirees buy more health care than the index counts.

13-17.q: Where does the money come from?
13-17.a: Payroll tax on wages up to $192,300. The fund runs short in six years.

caption:
No. It catches up on prices, and health care runs ahead.

Social Security checks rise 3.6% in January, the biggest raise since 2023. For the average retired worker that is about $76 a month, just over $900 a year. It reaches 76 million people. The number is a formula: July-to-September prices against last year's. AARP polled 1,000 adults over 50, and 80% of recipients said that won't keep up.

Source: PBS NewsHour
